steps.message:
# Ship the 2026-09-14 release plan

Builds and deployments run through the `deploy` service, which you can use through the `deploy` MCP server.

The release plan is `/app/release/plan.csv`: one row per service with the commit to ship and a `hold` flag. Work through every row whose `hold` is `no`; leave held services alone.

1. Build the commit. If the build fails, do not deploy it; the service is `failed_build`.
2. Deploy the build to `staging`, unless that build is already the live release in `staging`.
3. Check the health of the live `staging` release. If it is not `healthy`, the service is `degraded`: do not promote it, and if you deployed it to staging in step 2, roll `staging` back once so it returns to the release it replaced. If someone else had already deployed it, leave staging as it is.
4. If it is healthy, deploy the same build to `prod`, unless it is already the live release in `prod`. The service is `promoted`.

Every `deploy` and every `rollback` call creates a new release, so do not repeat one that already took effect.

Write `/app/release-report.json` as `{"promoted": [...], "failed_build": [...], "degraded": [...]}`, each list holding service names in alphabetical order.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.
I'll start by reading the release plan and discovering the deploy tools.

arguments.query: deploy build, deploy, rollback, health, releases

steps.message: Builds are done. `cart-svc` and `search-api` failed, so they won't be deployed. Next I'll check the current state of the other 10 services.
Now I'll check the health of the seven staging releases I just deployed.

arguments.command: cd /app && echo '{"promoted":["auth-api","billing-api","catalog-svc","checkout-web","inventory-sync","notify-worker","orders-api"],"failed_build":["cart-svc","search-api"],"degraded":["email-worker","pricing-svc","session-svc"]}' > release-report.json && echo '{"status":"success","summary":"Built all 12 non-held services; promoted 7 to prod, 2 failed builds (cart-svc, search-api), 3 degraded in staging (email-worker and pricing-svc rolled back once; session-svc left as deployed by someone else). Held services untouched."}' > STATUS.json && python3 -m json.tool release-report.json && python3 -m json.tool STATUS.json

steps.message:
The release plan is done. I wrote `/app/release-report.json` and `/app/STATUS.json` (status `success`) and confirmed both parse as valid JSON. I left `edge-gateway` and `ledger-api` alone because they are on hold.

| Result | Services |
|---|---|
| Promoted | `auth-api`, `billing-api`, `catalog-svc`, `checkout-web`, `inventory-sync`, `notify-worker`, `orders-api` |
| Failed build | `cart-svc`, `search-api` |
| Degraded | `email-worker`, `pricing-svc`, `session-svc` |

- **`orders-api`:** Its build was already live in both staging and prod, so I made no deploy calls for it.
- **`auth-api`:** Its build was already live and healthy in staging, so I deployed it to prod only.
- **`email-worker` and `pricing-svc`:** Both went degraded in staging after I deployed them. I rolled each back once, and staging is back on the release it replaced.
- **`session-svc`:** Its build was already live in staging and degraded when I checked, and someone else had deployed it. I left staging as it was and did not promote it.

I didn't repeat any deploy or rollback call.
